CHR has been widely applied in database management, event systems, constraint solving, and more recently, to model biological systems. This work introduces a novel method for compiling CHR programs into Constraint Logic Programming over Herbrand terms (CLP($\mathcal{H}$)) programs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this compilation technique by applying it to various models of real biological systems. Furthermore, we provide an implementation of the method within the CHRoCLP system, which supports the CLP($\mathcal{H}$) calculus and facilitates the modeling of biological systems using both CLP($\mathcal{H}$) and CHR. The paper concludes with experimental results that validate the efficiency of the compiled programs and the capability of the modeling language. This paper introduces a novel method for organ segmentation that leverages a limited set of annotated images alongside a small group of experts. However, current research on autonomous driving often overlooks the critical role of communication, leading to a scarcity of studies that integrate communication and control within a unified framework. This paper introduces a communication-controlled co-design approach that leverages the interplay between vehicle communication and control systems to maximize performance. We establish a unified Markov decision process (MDP) framework that encapsulates both communication and control elements, treating communication policy as a decision to be optimized. Subsequently, we develop an end-to-end deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm to derive the optimal joint policy for both subsystems. The proposed co-design method is evaluated in the context of connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs) utilizing vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication to exchange driving data. Simulation results demonstrate that this co-design approach significantly outperforms conventional methods that treat communication and control as separate, independent systems. Furthermore, the proposed approach exhibits robustness against communication failures and delays. Finally, we extend this co-design methodology to scenarios involving multiple CAVs, where vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication is employed to facilitate interactions among multiple CAVs. Simulation outcomes indicate that the co-design strategy yields substantial performance improvements over traditional approaches. In summary, this study underscores the necessity of jointly optimizing communication and control systems to fully harness the potential of communication-enabled autonomous driving. The source code for the proposed method is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYuan1995/CommCtrlCoDesign.

examines a scenario where a cache of size $K$ is utilized to serve a sequence of requests. While the actual requests remain hidden, the cache receives a stream of predictions regarding them. The objective is to minimize the cost of updates required to keep the cache current, aiming to achieve performance that is within a constant factor of the optimal strategy using the true requests. This study investigates the conditions under which such predictions must be provided to attain this level of performance. We demonstrate that predictions based on the true request distribution alone are insufficient for achieving constant-factor approximation. Instead, we prove that knowledge of the specific algorithm used to generate the predictions is necessary, thereby enabling the construction of constant-factor approximation algorithms for both Markov and i.i.d. request distributions. Furthermore, we present matching lower bounds for both settings, proving that a constant-factor approximation is unattainable when only the true request distribution is available. Additionally, we explore the scenario where the request distribution is unknown, introducing a novel algorithm capable of achieving a performance guarantee of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{K})$ relative to the optimal offline cache replacement algorithm using the true requests. Finally, we extend these findings to a more complex setting where requests are generated by a distribution conditioned on the history of cache updates. Our results indicate that, in this context, the only viable approach is to emulate an optimal offline algorithm using the available predictions. This extension is particularly significant as it demonstrates that even a minor amount of adaptivity can render the problem significantly harder. Notably, our algorithms are all online, deterministic, and require no knowledge of $K$. Moreover, they are highly practical, relying on straightforward data structures and algorithms, and can be effectively implemented in real-world systems. Finally, we conclude by outlining several natural directions for future research. This work is a condensed version of our findings, which are comprehensively detailed in the full technical report [1]. This study examines the strong decay properties of doubly heavy tetraquarks with flavor configurations $[cc\bar{c}\bar{u}]$ and $[cc\bar{c}\bar{s}]$ situated between two meson-meson thresholds. Employing the constituent quark model, we establish the spin-parity assignments for these states. Subsequently, we analyze their strong decay channels via the hadronic loop mechanism, incorporating both Coulomb and one-gluon exchange interactions alongside linear confinement within diquark-antidiquark clusters. Our findings indicate that the $[cc\bar{X}]$ ($X=u,u$ or $s$) tetraquarks can be identified through their decays into $D^{(\ast)}D^{(\ast)}$ or $D^{(\ast)}_sD_s$. This approach allows for the study of the system's behavior across both the short and long time regimes. The short-time regime is characterized by the ratio $N/\Delta t$, while the long-time regime is defined by $s$. The analysis examines the transition between these two regimes as a function of $N/\Deltat$ and investigates the dependence on the parameter $s$. Furthermore, the influence of the number of windings is examined. The chaotic nature of the graph is confirmed by observing level repulsion in the short-time regime and a linear growth of $K(s,\Delta t)$ in the long-time regime. Additionally, the fluctuations of $K(s,\Delta t)$ are analyzed in the long-time regime, revealing that they follow a Gaussian distribution. Finally, the study reports the emergence of a plateau in $K(s,\Delta t)$ within the long-time regime. This plateau appears at a height of approximately $1/3$ and occurs at a value of $s$ roughly proportional to $N$. The findings are compared with predictions from random matrix theory. The research is conducted within the framework of the Bohigas-Giannoni-Schmit conjecture. Additionally, the influence of the graph's Hamiltonian is analyzed. The study also examines the behavior of $K(s,\Delta t)$ as a function of $s$ for various values of $N$. Finally, the results are compared with those obtained from random matrix theory. The study demonstrates that the spectral statistics of quantum graphs can be effectively described by the spectral form factor $K(s,\Delta t)$. This factorization simplifies the analysis of the system's behavior across both short and long time regimes. This paper introduces a methodology for designing decentralized controllers for linear time-invariant (LTI) systems that are not necessarily NI, ensuring closed-loop stability while maintaining the NI property in the resulting decentralized interconnected system. The proposed approach relies on the existence of a specific type of decentralized positive real (DPRe) transfer function matrix (TFM), which is established through a linear matrix inequality (LMI) condition. Furthermore, the NI property of the controlled system is guaranteed by designing the controller as the negative of a decentralized positive real (NPR) TFM, where the previously defined DPRe TFM serves as a component. The study includes a numerical example to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed method. Additionally, the paper presents NI feedback interconnection-based decentralized control strategies for two classes of nonlinear systems, including those with unknown dynamics, utilizing the designed decentralized NI controllers. Simulation results are provided to validate the effectiveness of these nonlinear control designs. The work concludes by outlining open problems and future research directions. Finally, it is worth noting that this research was inspired by the authors' participation in the 2019 IEEE Control Systems Applications Competition (CSAC 2019), where their solution was ranked first among all submitted approaches. This paper investigates the joint optimization of transmit beamforming and IRS reflection coefficients to minimize energy consumption in multi-user multiple-input single-output (MIMO) systems. To address the resulting non-convex problem, we introduce a sequential optimization strategy. Furthermore, the study reveals that increasing the magnitude of the reflection coefficients can enhance the energy efficiency of the multi-user MIMO system. Our approach relies on a comparison with an independent SOS model, utilizing a coupling technique that extends the analysis presented in [BSS19]. Specifically, we establish that the decay of the transition probability between two fixed configurations is uniform across all times and configurations. This finding is derived by examining the SOS model restricted to a "tube" of fixed radius, where the number of valid configurations remains finite. Additionally, we illustrate how this result applies to the dimer model. Specifically, we prove that for a dimer configuration with a fixed height function, the conditional distribution of a specific height function, given the boundary height, exhibits Gaussian tail behavior. This conclusion is achieved by examining the count of dimer coverings within a tube of fixed radius. Furthermore, we confirm that the height function of the dimer model constitutes a SOS model. Consequently, our primary result regarding the SOS model yields a comparable outcome for the dimer model. This condition requires $f$ to be uniformly continuous with respect to a uniform structure $\mathcal U$ on $X$, which admits no more than a countable number of ultrafilters orthogonal to it. We demonstrate that this result applies to any compactification of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Furthermore, we examine the properties of the continuous extension of a function $f$ from a compact space $X$ to its maximal compactification $\bar{X}$. Specifically, we characterize the uniform structures on $X$ that ensure every filtered ultrafilter is non-orthogonal to continuous functions $f:X\to\mathbb{R}$, thereby allowing for the continuous extension of these functions to $\bar{X}$. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the compactifications of $X$ and $\bar{X}$, showing that the one-point compactification of $\bar{X}$ remains a compactification of $X$. Finally, we prove that the Stone-Čech compactification of $X$ corresponds exactly to the maximal compactification of $X$. In the concluding section, we address the case where $X$ is a compact metric space. We show that if a uniform structure $\mathcal U$ on $X$ is finer than the metric uniform structure, the uniform continuous extension theorem holds for $\mathcal U$. Moreover, if $\mathcal U$ is the uniform structure induced by a non-Archimedean metric, the compactification $\bar{X}$ is a zero-dimensional space. In this scenario, the continuous extension of $f$ to $\bar{X}$ is uniquely determined by its values on $X$. We also provide a characterization of the continuous extension of $f$ to $\bar{X}$ using clopen sets. Lastly, we note that the uniform continuous extension theorem does not hold for the uniform structure of the discrete metric on $X$. Consequently, the maximal compactification of $X$ under the discrete metric is the discrete space $X$ itself. Consequently, the continuous extension of a function $f:X\to\mathbb{R}$ to this maximal compactification is simply the continuous extension of $f$ to $X$. The system is engineered to capture nearly 100% of primary protons with kinetic energies below 10 MeV, while simultaneously deflecting particles with energies exceeding 1 MeV. The target chamber is cooled to cryogenic temperatures using liquid nitrogen, ensuring the target gas remains in a liquid state. This design choice minimizes the number of windows required to introduce the beam, thereby reducing energy loss and angular deflection of the primary protons. Additionally, the magnetic field configuration facilitates the collection of secondary particles with energies greater than 1 MeV, achieving an efficiency of approximately 80%. The system's performance has been evaluated using a 10 MeV proton beam, and the resulting data have been compared against predictions from the Geant4 simulation software. The results demonstrate that the actual performance aligns closely with the simulations. Furthermore, the new target system has been utilized to measure the cross section for the $^{12}$C$(p,\gamma)^{13}$N reaction. This measurement, conducted at proton energies ranging from 1 MeV to 10 MeV, is compared against existing literature data and the theoretical predictions of the REAC/MP code. The findings indicate that the measured cross section is consistent with both the REAC/MP model predictions and the results from other studies. Consequently, the newly developed target system is deemed suitable for the inverted recoil-in-flight measurement of the $^{12}$C$(p,\gamma)^{13}$N reaction. Future research will involve measuring the cross section for the $^{13}$C$(p,\gamma)^{14}$N reaction using this system. The underlying design concept is anticipated to be applicable for measuring other $(p,\gamma)$ reactions involving stable targets. The target's performance, as demonstrated in this work, is expected to be comparable to or superior to that of other existing gas targets. The target system is currently operational and ready for use. The accompanying video illustrates the new target system, the associated beamline, and the recoil catcher. This study investigates the dynamical evolution of a stellar system within a SMBH potential, incorporating the effects of stellar collisions. We examine the influence of the stellar mass function, the initial configuration, and the system's proximity to the SMBH. Our findings indicate that, regardless of the initial conditions, the system undergoes rapid dynamical relaxation, resulting in a centrally concentrated core of massive stars. This process generates a significant amount of X-ray radiation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that stellar collisions are a common occurrence in these systems, with their frequency increasing as the system approaches the SMBH. These collisions can produce black holes with masses ranging from stellar to intermediate scales. Consequently, compact stellar systems near SMBHs serve as a promising source of X-rays and a potential channel for SMBH mass growth. Additionally, they may contribute to the population of intermediate-mass black holes. The dynamical evolution of these systems is also expected to impact the surrounding interstellar medium. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the formation of intermediate-mass black holes. Our results suggest that such black holes could form through dynamical evolution in compact stellar systems, particularly those located near SMBHs. This mechanism could explain the existence of intermediate-mass black holes in various environments, including UCDs, GCs, and dwarf galaxies. Ultimately, our research offers new insights into the formation and evolution of compact stellar systems and black holes. We hope this study will stimulate further research into the dynamical evolution of these systems and their role in the formation of black holes. Furthermore, we find that stellar collisions are a common occurrence in these systems, with the collision rate increasing as the system approaches the SMBH. The methodology is versatile, accommodating both composite and simple hypotheses, as well as tests against specific parametric families like Pareto or Pareto mixture models. Furthermore, our approach remains asymptotically valid even when the underlying population variance or mean is infinite. We establish the limiting distribution of the test statistic and derive necessary and sufficient conditions on the tail index for asymptotic power. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed test achieves higher power compared to existing methods. Finally, we assess the performance of this test through extensive Monte Carlo simulations and an empirical analysis of real-world data. Simulation results indicate that the test maintains the correct rejection rate under the null hypothesis and exhibits superior power relative to alternative procedures. The application to real data confirms that the proposed test outperforms competing methods in detecting departures from the hypothesized model. Furthermore, we illustrate that the test is highly sensitive to detecting changes in the tail index. In summary, the proposed test offers advantages over current approaches, particularly in scenarios involving extreme tail heaviness. Consequently, we recommend this new testing procedure for practical applications. INTRODUCTION The study of black holes has been a central focus in gravitational physics for decades, with significant progress driven by the development of general relativity and its numerous extensions. However, despite these advancements, the fundamental nature of gravity remains an open question. While general relativity accurately describes gravitational phenomena at large scales, it fails to account for certain specific effects. This limitation has motivated the exploration of various modified gravity theories, including higher-order gravity, $f(R)$ gravity, and nonlocal gravity. Among these, nonlocal gravity has garnered particular attention due to its potential to address cosmological issues such as dark energy and dark matter. In this work, we examine the stability of black holes within a specific class of nonlocal gravity theories. Our analysis reveals that small black holes are marginally stable, while larger black holes exhibit stability. Furthermore, we analyze the thermodynamic behavior of these black holes, confirming that they satisfy the second law of thermodynamics. This finding extends the observation that Kummer decomposition exists for all degree $p^k$ isogenies when $k$ is odd. Consequently, the findings in this paper encompass the results previously established for quadratic Darbaxian systems. Moreover, the results presented herein are applicable to the general class of quadratic Darbaxian systems, including those that are not quadratic. Finally, the discussion includes the existence problem for isochronous centers in quadratic Darbaxian systems, confirming that such systems exist and that their existence cannot be fully characterized using only algebraic conditions. This conclusion follows from the fact that the system parameters constituting the set of isochronous centers cannot be entirely described by algebraic conditions alone. We analyze the spectrum of the finite torus approximation for these operators and estimate the rate at which these spectral values converge to the continuous spectrum. Our analysis reveals that the convergence rate is governed by $\min\{\log(1+||A-B||), \log(1+||B-A||^{-1})\}$, indicating that both A and B must be close to each other for optimal spectral approximation. for dark matter. The minimal dark $SU(2)$ model, which incorporates a dark Higgs boson, is the simplest framework supporting a dark fermion doublet. In this setup, the dark fermion dark matter (DM) candidate can be a mixture of Majorana and Dirac states, with the dark Higgs boson decaying into either dark fermion Majorana pairs or Dirac pairs. We examine the current constraints on this model, focusing on the decay of the dark Higgs boson into dark fermion pairs. Additionally, we investigate the production of dark fermion DM pairs at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) via vector-like quark (VLQ) pair decays, noting that the VLQs must be sufficiently heavy to evade LHC limits. We also analyze the decay of dark fermion DM pairs at LHC energies, considering the dark fermions to be nearly on-shell. Our findings indicate that while the decay of dark fermion DM pairs into Standard Model particles is heavily restricted, the decay of dark fermion-antifermion pairs within the invariant mass range of approximately $2m_{\chi}\pm 100$ GeV remains unconstrained. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the decay of dark fermion DM pairs can be suppressed by introducing a small dark U(1) gauge interaction. Finally, we explore the impact of the dark fermion's electric charge on the decay of dark fermion-antifermion pairs. We conclude that the dark fermion DM candidate within the minimal dark $SU(2)$ model is viable and could be detected at the LHC. The constraints on the model parameters are primarily driven by the decay of dark fermion DM pairs. We also discuss the possibility of extending this model to include multiple dark fermion families. The analysis is conducted using the MadGraph5\_MC\_NLO Monte Carlo event generator. This research is part of the Higgs, Dark Matter, and New Physics (HDNP) working group at the HEPMP2021 conference. This paper introduces a new class of $C^1$ spline interpolants that satisfy the boundary conditions of the linear functional $L(f) = \int_a^b f(x)dx$. Additionally, we show that incorporating a penalty term for the jump in the second derivative into the data fitting process results in even better performance. This paper examines the well-posedness of the wave equation for a homogeneous, isotropic, and linearly elastic medium, where the boundary conditions are defined by a symmetric $3\times 3$ operator. We demonstrate that these boundary conditions ensure well-posedness if and only if the operator is positive definite. Furthermore, we provide a framework for solving the wave equation using spherical wave expansions, specifically for cases where the boundary takes the form of a sphere. This approach is particularly valuable for applications involving spherical wave propagation, such as seismology. We apply this method to solve the wave equation with Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions, deriving Green's functions for both scenarios. Finally, we validate the accuracy of these solutions by comparing them against analytical results. Additionally, we outline a procedure for solving the wave equation with general boundary conditions by extending the spherical wave expansion method. We conclude by presenting numerical examples of wave propagation in a homogeneous, isotropic, and linearly elastic medium under various boundary conditions. These examples illustrate how boundary conditions influence wave propagation and offer a means to determine the wave speed within the medium. The provided code facilitates the solution of the wave equation in spherical coordinates for any boundary condition, enabling the analysis of wave propagation in diverse scenarios. Physics (HEP) has become increasingly competitive, with only a small fraction of PhD graduates securing positions. This trend is largely attributed to the rapid expansion of other sectors, particularly technology, which now competes directly with HEP for talent. To address this, we have established a dedicated career services program designed to assist HEP graduates in securing employment across diverse industries. This paper outlines the findings from our recent efforts, covering a wide spectrum of career paths. We begin by examining the full range of possibilities available to HEP graduates, followed by a discussion of our program's structure and its alignment with these diverse outcomes. Furthermore, we present data on graduate employment trends and the specific career choices they make, while also detailing the lessons learned from our initial experiences. Our goal is to encourage other institutions to develop similar programs and to foster a broader, more inclusive perspective on career development within the HEP community. Additionally, this work aims to promote the adoption of a more holistic approach to career services across all particle physics institutions. Finally, we hope to inspire further research into the career trajectories of HEP graduates and the diverse opportunities they present. While recent efforts have utilized deep neural networks to capture intricate user preferences, these methods often lack interpretability and suffer from poor generalization when data is scarce. To address these challenges, we introduce a framework that employs a generative model to represent user preferences. This approach offers both semantic interpretability and enhanced generalization capabilities. Specifically, we propose a novel user preference modeling technique based on Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) within the context of sequential recommendation. By learning a latent user preference space, our method enables the disentanglement of user preferences from input data. Furthermore, we develop a plug-and-play module that integrates these disentangled preferences into a standard recommendation framework. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance across various baseline models. In this scenario, the matrix $A$ is treated as a random variable, and the objective is to construct a decoder that operates without prior knowledge of $A$'s realization. This approach is particularly valuable in applications where the matrix $A$ is unknown at the receiver, such as in physical channels. This paper investigates the information-theoretic limits of such decoding within a framework where the decoder lacks knowledge of $A$. Specifically, we examine the random erasure channel, where the input $X$ is a vector of i.i.d. Bernoulli(1/2) random variables, and the output $Y$ is a subsequence of $X$ with a random erasure probability $\delta$. We demonstrate that for any $\delta < 1/2$, a decoder can be designed to recover the input $X$ from the output $Y$ without knowledge of $\delta$, achieving a success probability of at least $1 - o(1)$ as the block length $n$ approaches infinity. This finding is significant because it reveals a phenomenon where the error probability of a Maximum Likelihood decoder remains constant regardless of the erasure probability $\delta$, whereas our proposed decoder exhibits error probabilities that vary with $\delta$. Furthermore, we establish that our result is optimal for any decoder lacking knowledge of $\delta$. Additionally, we extend these findings to the scenario where the decoder possesses partial information about $\delta$. Our results indicate that this partial knowledge substantially enhances the error performance of the decoders. Finally, we also present a corresponding result for the case where the matrix $A$ is fixed. In this setting, we show that the error probability of our decoder is independent of the specific realization of $A$, and we also demonstrate that allowing the decoder partial information about $A$ significantly improves error performance. Notably, our proposed decoders are computationally efficient, with a complexity of $O(n \log n)$. The paper also includes a detailed discussion on the relationship between our proposed decoders and the LASSO algorithm. We demonstrate that the next-to-leading order (NLO) QCD corrections to processes like $g g \to G^0 G^0$ (where $G^0$ represents a SM gauge boson) are substantial, indicating that NLO calculations are essential for accurately estimating the production cross-sections of heavy ALPs. Utilizing the POWHEG-RES$^{V2}$ code, we perform these NLO computations and subsequently conduct a phenomenological analysis of ALP production at the LHC. Our findings reveal that the NLO corrections significantly alter the expected event rates for heavy ALP discovery. Furthermore, we examine the implications of these results for ALP searches within the diphoton channel. Finally, we discuss the feasibility of detecting heavy ALPs at the LHC and outline the necessary strategies for future searches. These outcomes are expected to enhance the prospects for identifying heavy ALPs at future hadron colliders. Additionally, the methodologies and findings presented herein may offer valuable insights for calculating QCD corrections in other ALP production scenarios. This work extends the findings of arXiv:1801.00959, which addressed NLO corrections for heavy ALPs coupled to fermions. While that prior study concluded that NLO corrections are negligible for such models, the present analysis shows that when heavy ALPs couple to SM gauge bosons, these corrections become significant. Consequently, this study complements the previous work by extending the investigation to include heavy ALPs coupled to SM gauge bosons. The results herein suggest that heavy ALP searches should be broadened to encompass models featuring couplings to SM gauge bosons. Moreover, the techniques and insights derived from this analysis may prove useful for computing QCD corrections in additional ALP production channels. This manuscript is the second in a series addressing NLO corrections for heavy ALPs; the first part, published as arXiv:1801.00959, focused on ALPs coupled to fermions. The current paper addresses the complementary scenario involving ALPs coupled to SM gauge bosons. In this context, we find that the NLO corrections are substantial, contrasting with the fermion-coupled case. This indicates that the phenomenology of heavy ALPs is highly sensitive to the specific coupling type. Therefore, future searches for heavy ALPs should consider both couplings to SM fermions and SM gauge bosons.

in astrobiology. While the search for biosignatures is a primary objective for upcoming space missions, life on Earth offers a unique opportunity for direct study. However, the link between specific biosignatures and the presence of life is often ambiguous, as abiotic processes can mimic biological signals. This study examines the spectral characteristics of the most prevalent biosignature, methane, to assess its reliability as an indicator of life. By analyzing methane spectra from various terrestrial sources—including natural gas seeps, landfills, rice paddies, and cattle farms—we found that the spectral features of methane from biological origins are indistinguishable from those produced by nonbiological sources. Consequently, methane alone cannot serve as a definitive biosignature for life on Earth or exoplanets. Instead, a combination of multiple biosignature gases is required to effectively detect life on other worlds. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the reliability of biosignature gases is heavily influenced by the specific environmental conditions in which they are generated. This research underscores the necessity of understanding the formation mechanisms of biosignature gases to accurately interpret signals from Earth and exoplanets. Ultimately, this work highlights the intricate relationship between biosignatures and life, emphasizing that a comprehensive understanding of biosphere formation is essential for the future detection of life beyond Earth. \begin{abstract}
Software security is a critical concern for both developers and end-users, as vulnerabilities in software systems can lead to severe consequences. While numerous methods have been proposed to detect software vulnerabilities, most prior research has focused on identifying bugs within C/C++ code. In contrast, this paper addresses the detection of vulnerabilities in Android, an open-source ecosystem. We propose a systematic approach for vulnerability detection in Android applications using source code, specifically targeting the most prevalent vulnerability classes. Our methodology involves analyzing source code to identify code clones and vulnerability clones, which serve as indicators of vulnerability presence. We developed a novel method to detect vulnerability clones by analyzing the similarity between code clones and vulnerability instances. Additionally, we introduced a new metric to measure the effectiveness of these code snippets in detecting vulnerabilities. Our results show that the proposed method successfully identifies Android vulnerabilities. The performance of our approach was evaluated using real-world Android applications, achieving an F1 score of 0.84. The code implementation is available at https://github.com/ahmadreza139/AndroidVulDetect.
\end{abstract}

This collection includes 400 annual records of the Niño 3.4 index, 395 measurements of the Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI), and 395 data points for the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) across the contiguous United States. Utilizing this dataset, we investigated the lagged response to El Niño within the North American drought record. Our findings indicate that the 1968–80 El Niño event was the most intense on record, with its influence on North American drought peaking in 1969. While the 1968–80 El Niño and the 1969–80 drought are frequently linked, our analysis reveals that the drought's onset actually began in 1967. Furthermore, we observed that the 1967–80 drought was the most severe in the United States during the 1960s. These results suggest that the 1968–80 El Niño and the 1969–80 drought were not causally connected. Additionally, we propose that the 1967–80 drought was likely driven by a distinct climate pattern, such as a Pacific decadal phase shift. Ultimately, this dataset offers a valuable resource for researchers studying the impacts of El Niño on North American droughts. We conclude by discussing the implications of these findings for future climate change projections. Specifically, we explore how the 1967–80 drought might influence the frequency of future droughts in the United States. Our analysis suggests that if the Pacific decadal phase shifts back to its current state, the likelihood of droughts in the United States will decrease. Conversely, if the Pacific decadal phase shifts to its opposite state, the probability of U.S. droughts will increase. Consequently, our results highlight the necessity of monitoring Pacific decadal variability to forecast future droughts in the United States. To overcome these obstacles, PSNs can leverage the transformative potential of 6G technologies, such as massive connectivity, reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS), and edge computing. We demonstrate that these quantum graph states can be defined through specific quantum operators, known as generators, which are connected via a tensor product of the generators and a comultiplication map derived from the bialgebra structure. Furthermore, we establish that this framework is equivalent to an adjoint action of the generators and explore the connection to the quantum Clifford group. We also investigate the relationship between the bialgebra structure and the symmetries of the graph states, proving that these symmetries are connected through the adjoint action of the generators. Finally, we apply this framework to determine the stabilizer group of the quantum graph states. The primary motivation for this research is to leverage the underlying bialgebra structure to develop quantum graph states with applications in quantum error correction and quantum information processing. Specifically, we examine the Heisenberg and Weyl algebras as examples of bialgebras and analyze the corresponding quantum graph states. We also characterize the symmetries of these states and their connections to the Clifford group, concluding with an analysis of the stabilizer group. Ultimately, this paper aims to provide a comprehensive framework for constructing and analyzing quantum graph states, with potential applications in quantum error correction and quantum information processing. By utilizing bialgebras, we can develop more efficient and robust quantum error correction codes, which are essential for building large-scale quantum computers. Additionally, this work offers new insights into the structure of quantum graph states and their symmetries, which may facilitate advancements in quantum information processing. Overall, this research holds the potential to significantly impact the field of quantum computing. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper by summarizing the main results and discussing potential future directions. The paper is self-contained and accessible to readers with a background in quantum information theory and algebra. To ensure a smooth user experience, these platforms must adapt video quality to fluctuating network conditions, preventing disruptions like buffering or pixelation. This paper introduces a novel video streaming architecture that leverages the edge computing paradigm to enhance video quality. The proposed system comprises three key components: a video encoder, an edge network, and a video player. The encoder generates multiple video versions at varying bitrates, which are then replicated across geographically distributed edge servers. The video player is responsible for selecting the appropriate video stream based on the user's current network conditions. **1. Introduction**

In numerous scenarios involving the assignment of limited resources to many applicants, mechanisms are required to ensure that all applicants have an equal probability of being selected. A common approach to achieving this fairness is the use of a tie-breaker mechanism, which randomly assigns resources among applicants who are otherwise equally qualified. This paper investigates the impact of such mechanisms on hiring efficiency.

We model applicants as risk-averse, risk-neutral, or risk-loving, and analyze how tie-breaker mechanisms influence hiring efficiency. Our results indicate that when applicants are risk-averse, the mechanisms can either increase or decrease hiring efficiency. Specifically, if applicants are risk-averse, hiring efficiency improves if the mechanism is a lotto tie-breaker but decreases if the mechanism is a seniority tie-breaker. In both cases, hiring efficiency is maximized when applicants are risk-neutral. Additionally, we show that applying a socially optimal tie-breaker mechanism can simultaneously enhance both applicant welfare and hiring efficiency.

We conclude by discussing the implications of these findings for the University of California system.

**1.1. Tie-Breaker Mechanisms**

A tie-breaker mechanism is a procedure designed to assign resources to applicants when demand exceeds supply. These mechanisms are frequently employed in various contexts, such as assigning students to universities, allocating medical school slots, distributing medical equipment, and assigning tasks to workers. In all these instances, a tie-breaker mechanism ensures fairness by treating all applicants equally.

Under this strict definition, recent type IIB black hole solutions that rely on analytic continuation to reach the horizon do not qualify as black holes. Instead, we demonstrate that type IIB superstring theory possesses smooth, unitary black hole solutions that emerge through double analytic continuation. Within the framework of the AdS/CFT correspondence, these double-continued solutions correspond to thermal states in CFTs featuring non-trivial, unitary Hamiltonians. We derive the linearized magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) equations governing small perturbations in such a rotating, axisymmetric plasma. By applying a Fourier transform to these equations, we obtain a system of coupled ordinary differential equations (ODEs) for the perturbed variables. We then solve this system using the Chebyshev pseudospectral method. The resulting eigenfunctions and eigenvalues are analyzed to investigate the stability of the plasma. Our findings indicate that the rotation of the plasma can significantly enhance its stability. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the stability of both Alfvén waves and kink modes is heavily influenced by the axial magnetic field. Specifically, Alfvén waves are unstable when the axial magnetic field is weak, whereas kink modes exhibit instability under conditions of a strong axial magnetic field. Additionally, we show that increasing the rotation frequency generally promotes greater stability. Finally, we present a stability diagram that illustrates how stability varies with the axial magnetic field strength and the plasma's rotation frequency. These results are expected to be valuable for understanding magnetized plasmas in astrophysical contexts. This paper aims to demonstrate the connection between $\omega$-differentiability and standard forms of smoothness. Specifically, we establish that if a function $f$ belongs to the Hölder-Zygmund class $C^{\omega +1}$, then $f$ is $\omega$-differentiable. Conversely, we prove that if $f$ is $\omega$-differentiable for some $\omega > 1/2$, then $f$ belongs to $C^\omega$. These findings provide a comprehensive characterization of $\omega$-differentiability in terms of smoothness properties. As a practical application, we derive a criterion for $\omega$-differentiability based on the decay rates of the Fourier coefficients of $f$. Furthermore, utilizing this result, we demonstrate that if the Fourier coefficients of $f$ satisfy $|\hat{f}(n)| = O(|n|^{-\omega-1})$, then $f$ is $\omega$-differentiable. This outcome is significant because it offers a method for determining the $\omega$-differentiability of a function without requiring the explicit construction of its antiderivative. The primary instrument employed in our proofs is the Fourier multiplier operator. Additionally, we present a result concerning the Fourier series of functions in $C^\omega$ for $\omega > 1/2$, which extends a theorem by Fejér. Finally, we apply these findings to investigate the $\omega$-differentiability of the Weierstrass function. We show that if $f$ is a Lipschitz function, then $f$ is $\omega$-differentiable if and only if $f$ is a $C^\omega$ function. Consequently, we conclude that the Weierstrass function is not $\omega$-differentiable. This result is particularly striking given that the Weierstrass function is continuous and possesses a Fourier series that converges uniformly. We also provide a detailed analysis of the $\omega$-differentiability of the Takagi function. We prove that the Takagi function is $\omega$-differentiable if and only if $\omega < 1/2$. This finding is notable because, although the Takagi function is continuous, it is not differentiable in the classical sense. Finally, we examine the Fourier series of the Cantor function, demonstrating that it fails to be $\omega$-differentiable

The DPLL(T) architecture is a foundational component of modern Smt-Solvers, offering a systematic approach to combining boolean reasoning with decision procedures for decidable theories. This paper examines the role of non-strict theories within this architecture and discusses their implementation in our solver, cvc5.
Nonstrict theories are those that allow for the derivation of new constraints based on the satisfiability of a set of constraints, without requiring the construction of a complete decision procedure. These theories are particularly useful in applications where a complete decision procedure is not necessary, or where the decision procedure is too expensive to compute. Nonstrict theories are also useful in applications where the constraints are too large to be stored in memory.
In the context of Smt-Solvers, nonstrict theories are typically used to propagate constraints that are derived from the satisfiability of a set of constraints. For example, if a set of constraints implies that a variable must be true, then the propagator will add a constraint that forces the variable to be true. This allows the solver to make decisions about the satisfiability of the constraints without having to construct a complete decision procedure.
Nonstrict theories are also used to propagate constraints that are too large to be stored in memory. For example, if a set of constraints implies that a variable must be true, then the propagator can add a constraint that forces the variable to be true without having to store the entire set of constraints. This allows the solver to make decisions about the satisfiability of the constraints without having to store the entire set of constraints.

given a matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ and a signal $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $k$ non-zero entries, the objective is to identify a vector $z \in \mathbb{R}^n$ that is $s$-sparse and satisfies $A x = A z$. We demonstrate that for any matrix $A$ where $n \geq 2m$, there exists a construction requiring $m = \Omega(n/k + \log n/\log m)$ measurements. This lower bound aligns with the established upper bound of $O(k \log n)$, which is achievable via the greedy algorithm IHT. Consequently, our findings indicate that the current greedy algorithms for sparse recovery are optimal when the number of measurements is limited to $m = O(\log n)$. Furthermore, we establish a matching upper bound for the case where $A$ comprises $m$ random $\pm 1$ vectors, proving that $O(\frac{k \log n}{m})$ samples suffice to recover a $k$-sparse signal. This result is achieved by applying the greedy algorithm IHT to the matrix $A$ and its first $m$ columns. Additionally, we derive a lower bound of $\Omega(\frac{k \log n}{m})$ for the recovery of a $k$-sparse signal using $m$ random $\pm 1$ vectors, thereby proving the optimality of IHT in this context. Finally, we examine the computational complexity of sparse recovery, demonstrating that recovering a $k$-sparse signal from $m$ random $\pm 1$ vectors is NP-hard whenever $m \geq k$. This hardness result is derived by reducing the NP-complete problem of finding a satisfying assignment for a 3SAT formula to the sparse recovery problem. The primary contribution of this work is the proof of the optimality of the greedy algorithm IHT for sparse recovery. This conclusion rests on two pillars: first, the upper bound of $O(\log n)$ measurements for IHT, and second, the lower bound of $\Omega(\log n)$ measurements required for any algorithm. Together, these results confirm that IHT is optimal for sparse recovery. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents the upper and lower bounds for sparse recovery using the greedy algorithm IHT; Section 3 details the computational complexity of sparse recovery; and Section 4 offers a discussion of our results

This study introduces a novel technique for extracting and analyzing faint companions from these images, termed the Bayesian Adaptive Optics System (BADAPP). BADAPP functions as a fully Bayesian, non-parametric, and self-calibrating method for modeling point-spread functions (PSFs) in high-contrast imaging. It utilizes a non-parametric basis set to model the PSF, with the number of basis functions determined automatically via Bayesian model selection. The approach employs a hierarchical Bayesian framework to infer the probability distribution of companion parameters, including position, flux, and PSF properties, while simultaneously accounting for uncertainties in PSF parameters and stellar flux. BADAPP's performance was validated using both simulated and real data. In simulated data, it successfully recovered companions with contrasts as low as 1000:1, whereas it failed to detect companions with contrasts below 100:1. The method was applied to 100 high-contrast images from the GPI Key Program, which targeted 50 young stars. BADAPP identified 16 companions with contrasts better than 100:1, including 10 new detections. Additionally, it detected companions with contrasts between 100:1 and 200:1, which were previously missed by other techniques. The method also revealed that companions previously thought to have constant contrast across the bandpass actually exhibit significant variations. Furthermore, we examine how decoherence varies across different subregions and how decoherence factors influence the transition of these subregions from quantum to classical states. Our findings indicate that decoherence is more pronounced in smaller subregions and diminishes as the number of degrees of freedom increases. Additionally, we observe that decoherence factors are highly sensitive to the specific spatial subregions analyzed. Finally, we establish that the entanglement between the observed subregion and the rest of the system plays a crucial role in the decoherence process. These results offer new insights into the mechanism of field-induced decoherence and may prove valuable for future applications in quantum field theory and quantum gravity. In this context, we also explore the potential for decoherence to drive the emergence of classical spacetime. Moreover, these findings could be experimentally realized in various setups, such as in a one-dimensional quantum wire or within a quantum field within a cavity. In the latter scenario, the quantum field can be modeled as a collection of independent harmonic oscillators, and the decoherence factors can be determined by measuring the expectation values of the corresponding observables. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the quantum-to-classical transition in quantum field systems. In this regard, we show that decoherence can be used to identify the boundary between quantum and classical regimes in such systems. Moreover, we find that the system's behavior is highly sensitive to the decoherence factors, which are influenced by the specific subregions under consideration. Finally, we suggest that the interplay between entanglement and decoherence in quantum field systems could lead to new phenomena and applications in quantum information processing and quantum computing. In this regard, we propose that the use of quantum field systems as quantum information processors could offer new perspectives on the development of quantum technologies. high accuracy on training data is viewed as a positive outcome. However, this paper demonstrates that for a specific category of models, termed "generalization models," accuracy is actually detrimental. We introduce a straightforward algorithm capable of transforming any generalization model into a highly accurate one that simultaneously maintains its original generalization guarantees. We also investigate the converse: the extent to which accurate generalization models can convert their corresponding algorithms into generalization models. Our findings indicate that this reciprocal transformation is not always feasible. Furthermore, we demonstrate that generalization models can achieve extremely high accuracy even when they possess minimal predictive power, rendering their outputs nearly indistinguishable from random. Finally, we examine the implications of these results for the scientific validation of machine learning algorithms. Our conclusion is that generalization models can be made arbitrarily accurate, yet this accuracy may be entirely spurious. Consequently, relying on accuracy alone is a flawed method for assessing a model's quality. Instead, generalization-specific metrics are required to properly evaluate these models. We propose a specific metric that fulfills these criteria. We anticipate that these results will inspire further research into generalization models and the development of more effective metrics for them. Additionally, we suggest that the concepts of generalization models and their associated metrics could prove valuable in other domains, such as the social sciences. Finally, we note that the techniques employed to establish our results can be extended to address other significant challenges in machine learning. To our knowledge, this is the first paper to address this specific class of machine learning models. We hope this work will stimulate additional research in this promising area. The primary difficulty stems from the nonlinearity of the drift and the absence of a global Lipschitz condition on the diffusion term. We introduce a novel approach that combines the Feynman-Kac formula with the Kolmogorov backward equation to establish a link between the solution of the SPDE and the corresponding stochastic Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation. This connection facilitates the derivation of a crucial estimate for the SPDE's solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the solution to the stochastic HJB equation can be represented via a system of forward-backward stochastic partial differential algebraic equations (F-PBDAEs). Leveraging this finding, we prove the existence of a solution to the original SPDE. Finally, we examine the Markov property of the solution and extend our results to a generalized stochastic control problem. To validate our theoretical findings, we provide a numerical example. This work represents a significant advancement toward resolving the long-standing issue of establishing semi-global solutions for nonlinear SPDEs with multiplicative noise. Additionally, our results are applicable to a wide range of other nonlinear SPDEs. The study also presents new findings regarding the connection between stochastic control and SPDEs, as well as the relationship between stochastic Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations and F-PBDAEs. This study employs a theoretical framework to elucidate the reentrant superconductivity and its linked anomalous Hall effect. Additionally, we show that the Hall voltage remains persistent, a phenomenon attributed to the quantum Hall effect. These results provide a novel approach for investigating the topological magnetoelectric effect and highlight the potential for achieving persistent Hall voltage in superconductors. Ultimately, our theoretical model offers a pathway to achieve a quantum Hall effect in a topological insulator. The existence of this topological magnetoelectric effect, which is sensitive to superconductivity, suggests that it can be detected via persistent Hall voltage, providing a new method for its experimental verification. Consequently, our theoretical model not only clarifies the reentrant superconductivity in MnBi$_2$Te$_4$ but also offers a novel strategy for detecting the topological magnetoelectric effect. These insights are expected to advance the understanding of superconductivity in topological insulators. Finally, we propose that this theoretical framework can be experimentally validated using other topological insulators, such as Bi$_2$Se$_3$ and Bi$_2$Te$_3$. We anticipate that our theoretical model will facilitate the investigation of superconductivity in topological insulators. **Introduction**

Machine learning models are increasingly utilized in critical sectors such as healthcare, finance, and law. These applications demand that models not only be accurate but also adhere to fairness principles. However, achieving fairness often necessitates a trade-off with accuracy. While fairness can be enforced through data preprocessing, postprocessing, or model retraining, this paper specifically addresses fairness constraints applied during model retraining. Such constraints can be formulated as a regularizer, a loss function, or a constraint within the optimization problem. The stringency of these constraints can be controlled by a hyperparameter, which is typically tuned via cross-validation. This paper examines the effect of varying the optimal stringency of fairness constraints on model accuracy. We demonstrate that accuracy does not decrease monotonically with increased stringency; instead, it exhibits a non-monotonic relationship. This insight enables the development of an algorithm to identify the optimal stringency that maximizes accuracy while satisfying fairness requirements. Our proposed algorithm is model-agnostic, requires no extra training, and accommodates any combination of fairness constraints. Experiments validate the algorithm's effectiveness in achieving the best possible accuracy and fairness outcomes.

This model assumes that the quantum state at any time $t$ is a pure state, $|\psi(t)\rangle$, and that the output is a linear function of this state. However, this assumption is frequently violated in practice, as the actual quantum state may be mixed, represented by a density matrix $\rho(t)$, and the output may be non-linear. To address these limitations, we introduce a more general classical feedforward model that allows for both non-linear functions of the density matrix and mixed states. Specifically, we demonstrate that the performance of QRC relies on the interplay between the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the density matrix. This decomposition enables a more precise understanding of the dynamics governing the quantum reservoir. Finally, we present experimental results using a trapped ion quantum computer to validate our approach. Our findings indicate that the enhanced model provides a more accurate description of QRC performance than the traditional model, particularly in scenarios where the general assumptions are breached. Additionally, the proposed decomposition of the density matrix offers valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of the quantum reservoir. This research paves the way for future investigations into the dynamical properties of quantum reservoirs. This paper introduces a novel image classification framework that integrates convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with sparse representation models. The approach leverages the robust feature extraction capabilities of CNNs to generate patches, which are then utilized for sparse modeling. Furthermore, we propose a new sparse coding algorithm that simultaneously optimizes patch selection and the sparse representation model. Comprehensive experiments confirm that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in terms of classification accuracy. This study examines the third-order intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity in a two-dimensional spin-orbit coupled Dirac system. We derive a general formula for the Hall conductivity, which scales linearly with the Fermi energy near the Dirac point. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Hall conductivity is directly proportional to the imaginary component of the Dresselhaus spin-orbit coupling. However, this symmetry can be broken by strain, which typically induces band gaps in topological materials, thereby destroying the topological state. This study demonstrates that band gaps opened by strain can remain stable in a two-dimensional Dirac semimetal characterized by strong spin-orbit coupling. We identify a topologically protected gapped phase that persists across a wide strain range, exhibiting a gapped Dirac cone at the K point. This robust gapped state is defined by a change in the winding number of the Berry phase around the K point, transitioning from 1 to 0 as strain increases. Consequently, the band gap remains topologically protected against perturbations, including further strain. Additionally, we observe that the band gap is highly sensitive to strain, offering a mechanism for strain-controlled switching between topological and trivial phases. This capability enables the creation of a strain-controlled topological transistor, where the topological phase functions as the "on" state and the trivial phase as the "off" state. Finally, we show that this topological transistor can be integrated with a strain sensor, allowing for the detection of minute strain variations through measurements of the transistor's on/off ratio. This research establishes a foundation for developing topologically protected, strain-controlled electronic devices. The findings are applicable to various topological materials, including Dirac semimetals, Weyl semimetals, and topological insulators. Specifically, we investigate the Dirac semimetal Cd$_3$As$_2$, which displays Dirac cones at the K point under strain. This material is notable for its high strain tolerance, making it an ideal candidate for the proposed topological transistor. Furthermore, the proposed device could be applied to strain sensing in harsh environments, such as high-temperature settings. comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms governing the formation of multiphase flow structures remains elusive. This study introduces a novel methodology to elucidate the mechanisms behind multiphase flow structures and their evolution within a microchannel. The approach utilizes a fully-coupled fluid-structure interaction (FSI) model to simulate the interaction between multiphase flows and microchannel walls. The model's validity is confirmed by comparing its predictions with experimental data from a microfluidic device. The study demonstrates that the evolution of multiphase flow structures is driven by the interaction between the shear stress exerted by the fluid on the channel walls and the interfacial tension forces acting on the dispersed phase. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the shear stress experienced by the dispersed phase is primarily determined by the continuous phase. These insights offer a new perspective for investigating the evolution of multiphase flow structures in microchannels. Additionally, the proposed methodology is applicable to analyzing the evolution of dispersed phase structures in other microfluidic systems. Finally, this methodology can be extended to examine the evolution of multiphase flow structures in other microfluidic configurations. This paper investigates the size of the largest maximal b-matching that remains compatible with a collection of $k$ $n$-vertex graphs, where each graph has maximum degree $\Delta$ and edge count $E$. We establish lower and upper bounds for this maximum size, demonstrating that the problem is tractable when $k$ is small or $\Delta$ is large. Furthermore, we examine the scenario where each graph contains exactly one edge, a setting equivalent to finding a common edge cover within a family of $k$ graphs. Additionally, we provide a characterization of graphs where every pair within a family shares a common edge cover. Finally, we address the problem of identifying a matching compatible with at least one graph from a family of $k$ graphs, proving that this task is NP-complete. We also present a polynomial-time algorithm for a restricted variant of this problem. Collectively, these findings offer new insights into the challenges of finding matchings across multiple labeled graphs. This research holds significance for both graph theory and data mining, with potential applications in areas such as multiple sequence alignment. Specifically, the effects-m decomposition requires that conditioning on a specific mediator variable $M$ renders the treatment independent of the confounders given $M$. This study investigates the conditions under which $M$ serves as a valid confounder for the mediator $Y$ in the context of individual-level causal effects. We demonstrate that $M$ is a valid confounder if and only if $Y$ and $M$ are causally unlinked, meaning no path connects $X$ and $M$ that lacks a $Y$-v-structure. Furthermore, we examine the scenario where $M$ is a linear combination of $Y$ and other variables, deriving a necessary and sufficient condition for $X$ and $M$ to be causally unlinked. These results are illustrated through various examples. Finally, we analyze the relationship between causal unlinking and the back-door criterion, proving that causal unlinking is a strictly weaker condition. We also present a counterexample to show that causal unlinking does not guarantee the validity of the effects-m decomposition. Consequently, we establish that the conditions required for the effects-m decomposition are not entirely captured by the back-door criterion. Finally, we illustrate how causal unlinking can be utilized to identify valid confounders for $M$. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these findings. In summary, our results indicate that the conditions for the validity of the adjustment formula and causal unlinking are not equivalent, and that the conditions for the validity of the effects-m decomposition are strictly stronger than those for the adjustment formula. Therefore, the conditions for the validity of the effects-m decomposition cannot be fully characterized by the back-door criterion. Instead, the causal unlinking of $X$ and $M$ is a necessary and sufficient condition for the validity of the adjustment formula for $M$. These results are applicable to any directed acyclic graph. Additionally, we provide a Python package that implements the causal unlinking test. This tool allows users to determine whether a given variable $M$ is causally unlinked from the treatment $X$ and thus suitable for use in the adjustment formula for $M$. By applying the anomaly matching condition alongside the 't Hooft anomaly of the global symmetry, we demonstrate that the gauge theory possesses at least one massless singlet in its low-energy spectrum. This finding holds true for all $N \geq 3$, with the exception of the case where $N=2$. Furthermore, we explore the potential implications of this result for SUSY QCD-like models. The validity of our conclusion is confirmed through specific instances, including $N=5$ with three flavors, and $N=3, 4$ with four flavors. Additionally, we establish that this phenomenon is universal, extending to SUSY gauge theories with gauge groups $SU(N)$ and flavor symmetries $SU(m)$ or $U(m)$ for any $N \geq 3$, provided that $m \geq 3$. In these scenarios, the massless singlet is a meson composed of quarks. Our methodology relies on the most basic anomaly matching condition, the 't Hooft anomaly of the global symmetry, and the inequality $m \geq 3$. Consequently, our findings are applicable to a broad range of SUSY gauge theories. Notably, our results are derived without requiring the existence of a dynamical $U(1)_R$ symmetry, the presence of a R-charge anomaly, or the application of the superconformal index. These insights are expected to be valuable for future investigations into the low-energy dynamics of SUSY gauge theories. Finally, we present a conjecture regarding the low-energy dynamics of SUSY QCD-like theories with $N=2$. This conjecture posits that when the number of flavors is two, the theory flows to an infrared (IR) free theory, whereas when the number of flavors is six, the theory flows to a confining phase. We provide supporting evidence for this conjecture by analyzing specific cases, such as $N=2$ with two or six flavors. Ultimately, we conclude that our results are robust and hold significant importance for advancing the understanding of SUSY gauge theories. This study investigates the effect using a minimal model of water, where each molecule's state is binary (liquid or gas), and interactions are governed by a simple rule: a molecule freezes if its neighbors are in the gas phase. We demonstrate that this model exhibits the Mpemba effect and analyze its dynamics to explain the observation. Specifically, we show that the presence of gas-phase neighbors creates a bistable system with two stable states, enabling the water to exist in either phase. Furthermore, we prove that the liquid-to-gas transition is a first-order phase transition, resulting in two distinct equilibrium states characterized by different relaxation times. These findings indicate that the interplay between fast-relaxing and slow-relaxing equilibrium states is essential for the Mpemba effect in this model. Our results indicate that for a fixed centrality class, collision energy significantly influences the multiplicity of high-$p_T$ particles. Specifically, at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200$ GeV, the ratio of high-$p_T$ yields in $A+A$ versus $pp$ collisions decreases as the nuclear system becomes more peripheral. Conversely, at the higher $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=2.76$ TeV, this ratio remains nearly independent of the centrality of the $A+A$ system. We attribute this discrepancy to the distinct roles of parton-parton scattering and parton-nucleon scattering in the two energy regimes. Furthermore, we observe that the centrality dependence of the high-$p_T$ particle ratio is markedly weaker at LHC energies compared to RHIC energies. Finally, we demonstrate that the high-$p_T$ particle yields in $A+A$ systems are highly sensitive to the saturation scale. Consequently, our findings offer valuable insights into the multiplicity of high-$p_T$ particles produced by heavy ions at LHC energies. Additionally, our results suggest that the saturation scale at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=2.76$ TeV is substantially lower than at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=0.9$ TeV. These objects, known as hypervelocity stars (HVSs), are believed to be ejected from the Galactic center by interactions with the supermassive black hole, Sgr A*. This study examines the orbital characteristics of 12 HVSs, including 10 newly identified ones, and analyzes the distribution of their pericenter distances. The results indicate that 11 of these HVSs likely originated from the Galactic center, whereas one, designated HVS1, appears to have formed outside the central region. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the pericenter distances of HVSs are not uniformly distributed; instead, they exhibit a peak near 10 parsecs, suggesting that HVSs born closer to Sgr A* are more frequently ejected. This non-uniform pericenter distribution may serve as a valuable tool for investigating the Galactic center's structure and dynamics. Additionally, we find that the pericenter distances of HVSs correlate with their current velocities, implying that stars with higher present-day velocities were ejected from closer to Sgr A* than those with lower velocities. This relationship may aid in understanding the Galactic center's structure and dynamics. Finally, we explore the potential for using HVSs to measure the mass of Sgr A*. By analyzing the HVS velocity distribution, we estimate Sgr A*'s mass to be approximately $4.31 \times 10^6 M_\odot$, a value consistent with the $4.29 \times 10^6 M_\odot$ derived from stellar dynamics. This agreement supports the hypothesis that HVSs originate from the Galactic center. However, the discrepancy between our estimated mass and the value obtained from stellar dynamics may stem from the fact that our sample of 12 HVSs is not representative of the entire HVS population. Consequently, a larger sample of HVSs is required to accurately determine the mass of Sgr A*. This paper is the first to analyze the orbital properties of HVSs and the pericenter distance distribution, and it is the second study to estimate the mass of Sgr A* using HVSs. The first such study was conducted by Gao et al. (2021). We anticipate that this work will advance the study of hypervelocity stars. Introduction. Simulation-to-real learning has garnered significant attention in robotics, with the core objective being the transfer of knowledge from synthetic to real-world settings. A prevalent strategy involves aligning the feature spaces of both domains to ensure policies trained in simulation perform effectively in reality. This alignment is typically achieved by minimizing the discrepancy between observations and features, such as through adversarial learning or contrastive methods. However, these methods often fail to capture the complete information contained within observations. In this work, we propose a new algorithm that maximizes mutual information between features and observations to achieve robust simulation-to-real learning. Our approach is straightforward to implement and delivers superior performance compared to current methods.

Results. We evaluated our method against state-of-the-art baselines across various simulation-to-real learning tasks, including object manipulation, robot arm control, and bipedal walking. Our approach consistently outperformed the baselines, achieving higher success rates in all tested scenarios. Additionally, we conducted an ablation study to examine the impact of different configurations, confirming the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm.

This augmented image retains the original background while adding new foreground elements. We demonstrate that the cut-paste method surpasses other state-of-the-art augmentation techniques when evaluated on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets. Additionally, we present a straightforward yet effective post-processing strategy that further boosts the performance of models trained with this method. This paper introduces a framework that equips large language models (LLMs) with environmental knowledge by utilizing an external retrieval system. We present a method to enhance an LLM's reasoning capabilities by integrating an external knowledge base, ensuring that the model's knowledge is consistently up-to-date. This study presents the first detection of a transiting planet orbiting a white dwarf, designated WD 1145+017. The white dwarf has a mass of approximately 0.62 solar masses and a radius of roughly 0.018 solar radii. The transiting object, designated WD 1145+017b, has a mass of about 0.004 solar masses and an orbital period of 2.4 days. Its transit depth of 1.5% corresponds to a radius of approximately 0.015 solar radii, making it significantly larger than the white dwarf. The observed transit depth exceeds the white dwarf's cross-section by a factor of roughly 2.5, indicating that the transiting body is substantially larger than the star itself. Furthermore, the transits exhibit variability, varying by up to 50% in both depth and duration. We propose that WD 1145+017b is a disintegrating planetesimal, with the observed variability resulting from the stochastic ejection of dust. The system's transits are characterized by a high dust production rate of approximately $10^{10}$ grams per second and a rapid dust destruction timescale of roughly 10 hours. The dust production rate is estimated to be at least 100 times greater than that of KIC 12567518, a system with a similar transit profile. The transiting object is located approximately 100 astronomical units from Earth. We discuss the implications of these findings for the evolution of planetary systems around white dwarfs. The presence of such a system suggests that planets can survive the red giant phase and remain intact until the white dwarf phase, at which point they are destabilized and begin to disintegrate. Additionally, the high dust production rate implies that the system is in a late evolutionary stage, where the host star has recently transitioned to a white dwarf. The findings also suggest that the white dwarf phase is brief, with a duration of less than 100 million years. Finally, we discuss the potential for future discoveries of similar systems. The data presented in this paper are available in the supplementary material. The data are publicly accessible at the NASA Exoplanet Archive

band structure in the two-dimensional honeycomb lattice of atoms with mass $m_A$ surrounded by a hexagonal electron gas of mass $m_B$. This model, applicable to both bulk and monolayer systems, captures the essential physics of the recently synthesized van der Waals heterostructure of graphene on a hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) substrate. In this framework, the electron gas exerts a repulsive force on atoms of mass $m_B$ and an attractive force on atoms of mass $m_A$. We demonstrate that the resulting phonon band structure exhibits topological characteristics, including Dirac cones and flat bands, which are governed by the mass ratio $m_A/m_B$ and the electron-to-atom binding strength. Furthermore, we identify a topological phase transition within the phonon spectrum, characterized by the opening of a gap at a Dirac point. This transition occurs when the binding energy between atoms and the electron gas equals the difference in their free energies. Finally, we show that the topological nature of the phonon band structure can be tuned by adjusting the electron gas density. These findings are significant for the design of two-dimensional materials and devices featuring novel functionalities. In conclusion, this study reveals an intriguing topological phenomenon in hexagonal lattices where an electron gas interacts with atoms of distinct masses. This phenomenon is driven by the interplay between the mass ratio $m_A/m_B$ and the binding energy of the atoms to the electron gas. We anticipate that this topological effect will facilitate the development of new materials and devices with unique properties. This paper presents a method for determining $\gamma$ within a $B_s^{\ast}$ decay chain that achieves a precision of approximately $0.1^\circ$. The technique relies on a decay chain where a $B_s^{\ast}$ meson decays into a $B_s$ meson and a photon, with the $B_s$ subsequently decaying into a $D_s^{\ast}$ and a $K^{\ast}$, the $D_s^{\ast}$ then decaying into $D_s$ and a pion, and finally the $D_s$ decaying into $K^{\ast}$ and $K^-$. By utilizing the spinor structure of the $B_s^{\ast}$ decay, the phase of the CKM angle $\gamma$ can be extracted with high accuracy. The $B_s^{\ast}$ mass is reconstructed from the $B_s\gamma$ system, while the $B_s$ mass is independently reconstructed from the $D_s^{\ast} K^{\ast}$ system. This dual mass reconstruction enables the determination of the $B_s^{\ast}$ mass shift relative to the $B_s$ mass, a critical component for the high-precision extraction of $\gamma$. The study also examines the impact of CP violation in the $D_s^{\ast}$ decay and the CP violation of the $B_s^{\ast}$ mixing amplitude on the extraction of $\gamma$. Furthermore, the analysis includes the $B_s^{\ast}$ mass shift and the $B_s^{\ast}$ mixing amplitude within the decay chain. The results indicate that the $B_s^{\ast}$ mixing amplitude is negligible, and the $B_s^{\ast}$ mass shift is negligible when the $B_s$ mass shift is accounted for. Consequently, the $B_s^{\ast}$ mass shift is not required for the $\gamma$ extraction. Finally, the paper discusses the feasibility of detecting the $B_s^{\ast}$ mass shift in the $D_s^{\ast} K^{\ast}$ decay channel at the LHCb detector. The findings suggest that the $B_s^{\ast}$ mass shift is observable in the LHCb detector with a precision of about 1 MeV.

However, the absence of a suitable modulation scheme has hindered its practical application. This paper introduces FTN signaling utilizing the Hadamard matrix, termed Hadametz, and demonstrates that it can achieve arbitrarily high data rates. We derive a closed-form expression for the Hadametz signal's autocorrelation function and subsequently formulate the FTN problem as a quadratic optimization task. To address this, we propose a low-complexity iterative algorithm that converges to the optimal solution. Simulation results confirm that the proposed Hadametz scheme can reach any target rate with negligible bit error rate. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Hadametz can attain a higher maximum data rate compared to conventional Nyquist signaling. Finally, Hadametz exhibits superior performance relative to other FTN methods, such as the widely used FTN-QAM, in terms of both bit error rate and computational complexity. The proposed iterative algorithm is easily implementable and can be readily integrated into existing communication systems. Consequently, the study of Hadametz and this iterative approach may offer valuable insights for the development of future FTN signaling schemes. This paper introduces a method for generating $N$-qubit entanglement using a universal gate that links two qubits to an ancillary system of $N$ qubits. Our findings indicate that the single-step generation of $N$-qubit entanglement is a highly efficient resource for quantum algorithms.
